system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, morbid obesity, and peripheral vascular disease was admitted with fever and an infected right internal jugular hemodialysis catheter. She met criteria for severe sepsis and was found to have MRSA bacteremia. The infected catheter was removed, and a temporary femoral line was placed, later converted to a tunneled left femoral catheter after failed attempts to recanalize the right jugular vein. She was treated with vancomycin, and blood cultures cleared. Concerns for endocarditis and osteomyelitis were ruled out with TEE and clinical monitoring. Constipation and back pain resolved during admission. Warfarin was held during procedures and restarted with heparin bridging until INR was therapeutic. She was discharged to extended care for ongoing dialysis and outpatient antibiotic therapy with close monitoring.
problems: Other and unspecified infection due to central venous catheter
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. You came in with nausea and feeling unwell—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this nausea for about a week. I’m not throwing up, but I just feel off. I also have a dry cough and last night I had bad night sweats.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, belly pain, or changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No belly pain. I did have a bowel movement yesterday after taking milk of magnesia, but before that I can’t remember when. I’ve been constipated for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your labs and your potassium was high earlier, but it’s better now. Your kidney function is stable with dialysis. We also saw a shadow on your chest X-ray, so we started antibiotics just in case it’s pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know. But I feel hungry now—does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. You’re not in distress, and your breathing is fine. We’ll keep monitoring. We also noticed a rash on your lower back—does that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s sore and itchy. I’ve had it for a while, but it hasn’t healed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care looked at it and thinks it’s a fungal rash with a small skin crack. We’re going to start an antifungal cream and make sure you’re not sitting on it too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your infection markers are normal, and the chest X-ray shadow is likely old. We’re stopping the antibiotics since it doesn’t look like pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the nausea isn’t from an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so. Your gallbladder ultrasound didn’t show any active issues, and your liver tests are stable. Given your history of reflux and obesity, we think it might be related to stomach acid. We’ve started you on omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—I’ve had heartburn before. But what about the mass in my breast? I’m worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. The mass needs follow-up with breast surgery. It could be serious, so please make that appointment as soon as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving, and you’re feeling better. We’re going to discharge you to extended care today where you can continue dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I keep taking the new medicine for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take omeprazole daily. Also keep using the antifungal cream for your rash, and don’t forget to follow up with dermatology. And please see the breast surgeon about the mass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep an eye on your weight—call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. Otherwise, you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’ll go to extended care today, and all your medications are listed, including insulin, warfarin, and the new omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking magnesium citrate for constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once a week, or more if needed. The polyethylene glycol and senna are also there to help. Stay on top of it—constipation can make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to follow up on everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re alert, eating, and your vitals are stable. We’re confident you’ll do well with the right follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than yesterday. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The transport team will take you to extended care shortly. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe transfer.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, morbid obesity, and a history of venous thrombosis was admitted for evaluation of persistent nausea and malaise. She had no abdominal pain or vomiting but reported a dry cough and night sweats. Initial concerns for infection led to a brief course of antibiotics, but imaging showed a chronic retrocardiac opacity unlikely to be infectious, and antibiotics were discontinued. Nausea was thought to be related to gastroesophageal reflux, and she was started on omeprazole. A sacral fungal rash with a fissure was identified and treated with topical ketoconazole. She remained stable, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing dialysis and outpatient follow-up for a breast mass, dermatology, and primary care. Her home medications, including warfarin, insulin, and constipation regimens, were continued.
